title: Global wind power: 4 things to know in H2 2026 and beyond | Wood Mackenzie
gist: Global wind is at an inflection: falling European onshore tender prices are set to deliver the first turbine cost reductions since 2020, while redesigned 20-year CfD-based offshore frameworks face a stress test in a packed 2026-27 tender calendar. In China, returns increasingly hinge on consumption routes, trading exposure and storage dispatch rather than volume built, and outside China an ageing, uneconomic-to-repower fleet keeps occupying prime sites.

themes.theme: European tender price deflation and turbine supplier margin squeeze

insights.claim: 2026 is on track to deliver the first wind turbine cost reductions since 2020, ending a multi-year run of cost inflation in the sector.
insights.speaker: Sasha Bond-Smith
insights.so_what: A turbine cost down-cycle changes project IRR math and turbine OEM revenue-per-MW assumptions; watch OEM pricing guidance and per-MW capex disclosures for confirmation.
insights.quote: Currently, 2026 is on track to deliver the first turbine cost reductions since 2020.

insights.claim: Rising volumes combined with intensifying competition are pushing winning prices for onshore wind tenders lower across leading European markets.
insights.speaker: Sasha Bond-Smith
insights.so_what: Falling clearing prices compress developer revenue per MWh even as volumes grow — volume growth is not automatically earnings growth for European onshore developers.

insights.claim: Turbine suppliers face a structural tension between cutting product cost to defend margins and continuing to fund development of the next generation of larger, more efficient turbines.
insights.speaker: Sasha Bond-Smith
insights.so_what: R&D underinvestment risk at OEMs is the second-order cost of tender price deflation — watch R&D-to-sales ratios and platform launch cadence at turbine makers.
insights.quote: For suppliers, this creates a tension between the pressure to deliver products at lower cost to help maintain margins and the need to invest in developing the next-generation of larger, more efficient turbines.

insights.claim: Cost inflation and geopolitical shocks have not been resolved for the wind sector, yet the forward outlook for wind generation is described as somewhat more positive than in recent years.
insights.speaker: Sasha Bond-Smith
insights.so_what: A cautious inflection call rather than an all-clear — position for improving generation economics without assuming input-cost relief is durable.
insights.quote: But while these issues haven’t gone away, the outlook for wind generation going forward looks somewhat more positive.

themes.theme: Offshore tender reform: risk transfer to governments, tested in 2026-27

insights.claim: Redesigned offshore wind tender frameworks are helping restore investor confidence following a series of failed tenders in 2024-25.
insights.speaker: Sasha Bond-Smith
insights.so_what: Failed-auction risk was the key repricing event of 2024-25 for offshore developers; framework redesign is the mechanism that reopens the pipeline.
insights.quote: Redesigned offshore wind tender frameworks are helping to restore investor confidence after a series of failed tenders in 2024-25.

insights.claim: The new offshore tender models centre on contracts for difference with durations of 20 years or more that shift risk from developers to governments, alongside new non-price criteria and supporting mechanisms such as the UK's Clean Industry Bonus.
insights.speaker: Sasha Bond-Smith
insights.so_what: Longer-dated, government-backed CfDs de-risk offshore cash flows and should lower cost of capital — but they move merchant and cost risk onto sovereign balance sheets, a fiscal exposure to monitor.
insights.quote: New models focus on contracts for difference (CfDs) that transfer risk from developers to governments, with durations of 20 years or more, new non-price criteria and supporting mechanisms such as the UK’s Clean Industry Bonus.

insights.so_what: The 2026-27 auction calendar is the near-term catalyst set for European offshore names — subscription levels and clearing prices are the read-through.

themes.theme: China: capacity targets versus consumption and return quality

insights.claim: China's Plan for Building a New Energy System, part of the 15th Five-Year Plan, sets a goal for wind and solar to exceed 50% of installed capacity by 2030.
insights.speaker: Sasha Bond-Smith
entities: Plan for Building a New Energy System
insights.so_what: A hard policy anchor for Chinese wind and solar equipment demand through 2030, supporting volume for domestic supply chains regardless of price.
insights.quote: The Chinese government’s Plan for Building a New Energy System sets a clear goal for wind and solar to exceed 50% of installed capacity by 2030.

insights.claim: Chinese onshore wind is booming while offshore wind faces challenges, and sustaining the onshore build pace will depend on securing credible routes to consumption rather than on capacity targets alone.
insights.speaker: Sasha Bond-Smith
insights.so_what: Curtailment and offtake are the binding constraint on Chinese wind, not installation capability — watch utilisation and curtailment rates, not just GW added.
insights.quote: While offshore wind faces challenges, onshore wind is booming. However, sustaining that pace will depend on securing credible routes to consumption.

insights.claim: With Chinese power prices now fully exposed to market trading and mechanism prices falling, developer returns will increasingly depend on trading exposure and storage dispatch rather than the sheer volume of capacity built.
insights.speaker: Sasha Bond-Smith
insights.so_what: The value driver in Chinese renewables shifts from GW installed to merchant trading and storage optimisation capability — favours operators with dispatch and storage assets over pure build-and-hold developers.

themes.theme: Ageing fleet and the weak economics of repowering outside China

insights.claim: Outside China, a decommissioning backlog in mature wind markets means an ageing and obsolete turbine fleet will keep occupying many prime generating sites well into the next decade.
insights.speaker: Sasha Bond-Smith
insights.so_what: Prime wind sites with grid access stay locked up by legacy assets, capping new-build opportunity and supporting the value of existing site rights.
insights.quote: Outside of China, the decommissioning backlog in mature wind markets means an ageing and obsolete turbine fleet will occupy many prime generating sites well into the next decade.

insights.claim: Advanced operations and maintenance, favourable power prices, high decommissioning and repowering costs, and limited policy incentives combine to weaken the business case for replacing older turbines.
insights.speaker: Sasha Bond-Smith
insights.so_what: Life-extension beats replacement under current economics — bullish for wind O&M and service revenue streams, bearish for near-term repowering turbine orders.
insights.quote: Advanced operations and maintenance, favourable power prices, high decommissioning and repowering costs and limited policy incentives weaken the case for replacing older turbines.

insights.claim: Overall wind fleet efficiency is expected to improve as the pace of repowering slowly accelerates, with the greatest gains concentrated at sites that have the best wind resources and grid access.
insights.speaker: Sasha Bond-Smith
insights.so_what: Repowering upside is site-selective, not sector-wide — value accrues to owners of top-decile resource and interconnection positions.
insights.quote: However, overall fleet efficiency is set to improve as the pace of repowering slowly accelerates, with sites boasting the best wind resources and grid access delivering the greatest gains.
